title: Suffering: A Bible Study for When Life Does Not Make Sense
subtitle: A five-session study on suffering, lament, and the God who doesn't explain but comes.
summary:
This study is for people in pain, for the people sitting near them who have run out of things to say, and for small groups willing to hold a hard question without rushing to close it. Its five sessions take the problem of pain at its full weight through Job; recover lament as faithful speech through the Psalms; come to the cross, where God answered suffering by entering it rather than explaining it; look at Paul's thorn and the grace that was enough when the thorn stayed; and end with the new creation, where God himself wipes away every tear. A volunteer can lead it with no training. Each question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

It refuses the sentences the church reaches for when it's uncomfortable, like "everything happens for a reason" and "God needed another angel," and it refuses just as firmly the despair that reads a wound as proof no one is there. It won't tell a person in agony that the answer is to trust more, or that their grief is a failure of faith. Where the pain has turned toward self-harm or despair that will not lift, the study says plainly that this is the moment to reach for a pastor, a counselor, a doctor, or a crisis line (in the US, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline), and to reach today. The gospel doesn't require anyone to suffer alone. The God at the center of this study wept at a grave he was about to open.
audience: Anyone in grief or pain, those walking with them, and small groups

sessions.title: The Question We Are Not Allowed to Ask
sessions.aim: To state the problem of pain at its full weight instead of defusing it early, to honor Job and the psalmists who put the hard question to God directly, and to refuse both the atheism that treats suffering as a closed case against God and the piety that won't let a sufferer ask why.
sessions.summary:
People a week past a funeral sometimes say the thing nobody is supposed to say in church: they don't want comfort, they want an explanation, and if God has one, they'd like to hear it now. Nobody has one to give. And the church has a drawer full of sentences that make the ache smaller: everything happens for a reason, God won't give you more than you can handle. Each one stops the person from asking the question.

The Bible doesn't flinch from that question. It wrote the sharpest version of it into its own pages. Job loses everything for no reason he is ever told, and for chapter after chapter he refuses his friends' tidy theology and demands that God answer him. The atheist's case is heavy here, and it deserves to be heard: a world with this much undeserved agony is hard to square with a God who is both good and able.

But God never gives Job the explanation. He gives Job himself. And Job says at the end, "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you" (Job 42:5). The problem of pain is real, and this study won't shrink it. The God it points to didn't send an argument into the world. He came.

keyScripture.why: "Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face" (Job 13:15). Trust that won't let go and protest that won't pretend, in one sentence.

discussion.q: "Everything happens for a reason." "God needed another angel." "He won't give you more than you can handle." Which of these has been said to you in pain, and what did it do?
discussion.behind: Start with experience, not theory. Most people who said these lines were frightened and kind, so don't mock them. Just let the room admit that the line usually ended the conversation the sufferer needed to have.

discussion.q: Read Job 13:15. How can Job say "I will hope in him" and "I will argue my ways to his face" in the same breath?
discussion.behind: This is the shape of Job's faith: he won't let go of God and won't pretend he's fine. Help the room see that both halves are faith.

discussion.q: Many thoughtful people say that a world with this much undeserved suffering is hard to square with a God who is both good and able. What's true in that objection that you don't want to lose?
discussion.behind: Don't let the room rush to answer it. This is the strongest argument against the faith, and a study that won't state it fairly hasn't earned the right to respond. Make sure any skeptic in the room hears it taken seriously.

discussion.q: Read Job 42:1-7. God never gives Job the explanation he demanded, only himself, and Job falls quiet. Why might presence satisfy Job when an answer might not have?
discussion.behind: The book withholds the reason on purpose. Don't resolve this too fast; for some in the room the answer hasn't come and presence hasn't yet felt like enough. Notice too that God rebukes the friends who explained, not Job who protested (Job 42:7).

discussion.q: When have you reached for a quick answer to ease your own discomfort with someone else's pain?
discussion.behind: Go first. Nearly everyone has filled a hard silence with a platitude. You can't sit well with a sufferer until you've admitted how often you've escaped their pain by explaining it.

objections.objection: The amount of pointless, undeserved suffering in the world is the clearest evidence there is no good God. A God who could stop a child's agony and doesn't is either not good or not real.
objections.response: This is the strongest thing an unbeliever says, and it shouldn't be brushed aside. The suffering is real, much of it is undeserved, and any answer that makes it small is an evasion. The Bible itself refuses that evasion by giving us Job. But notice what the objection assumes: that if there were a good God, he'd owe us an explanation we could follow. The book of Job looks straight at this problem and doesn't end with an explanation. It ends with God arriving, and the sufferer finding that what he most needed was not a reason but a presence. The objection is right that suffering is a real problem. It overreaches in concluding that a problem we can't solve means no one is there. The Christian claim is stranger: the one who is there didn't stay above the problem. He entered it, on a cross.

objections.objection: Telling people to just trust God and stop asking why is how the church silences hurting people and makes their grief feel like sin. Questioning God may be the most honest thing a person can do.
objections.response: The church has often done exactly this, and the harm is real. Hurting people have been made to feel that their questions were faithlessness, and the pressure has pushed them into pretending or out the door. That instinct doesn't come from Scripture. The Bible gives us Job, who argues his case to God's face and is approved for it (Job 42:7), a book of Psalms where about a third are complaints, and a Savior who cried from the cross, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34). What the study does ask is that the question be aimed at God, not away from him. Job kept talking to the God he was arguing with. That's the difference between lament and leaving.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What question about your own suffering, or someone you love, have you never let yourself ask God out loud? What are you afraid would happen if you did?
sessions.practice: This week, take the question you've been keeping from God, the "why" you've swallowed to seem faithful, and say it to him directly, out loud or on paper, without softening it. Don't answer it for him and don't apologize for it. Bring it to him the way Job did. Afterward, notice whether saying it pushed you further from God or, strangely, closer, and write down what you felt.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we've been taught to hide our hardest questions from you, as though you were too fragile or too far away to hear them, so we've carried them alone and called our silence trust. Forgive us the cheap answers we've handed to people in pain because their grief frightened us. Teach us to bring the real question to you, the way Job did, and to find that you would rather have our anguish than our polite distance. Where any of us is in a darkness that has grown dangerous, don't let us hide it. Send us people, and help us reach for them today. And meet us as you met Job, not with an argument but with yourself. Amen.
reflection: What quick answer to suffering have I believed or repeated, and what has it kept me from feeling, in myself or with others?
Do I believe God can bear my hardest question, or have I been protecting him, and myself, by never asking it?
When I'm near someone in real pain, do I sit with them, or reach for a sentence that makes me more comfortable and them more alone?
sessions.teaching:
People a week past a funeral sometimes say the thing you aren't supposed to say in church. They don't want comfort. They want an explanation, and if God has one, they'd like to hear it now. Nobody has one to give them, and the right thing is to say so and stay in the chair. But there's an instinct in that moment to make the ache smaller, and the church keeps a drawer of sentences for it. Everything happens for a reason. God needed another angel. He won't give you more than you can handle. However kindly meant, each one does the same thing: it ends the conversation the sufferer most needed to have.

So I don't want to start with an answer to suffering. I want to start with permission to ask. Everyone in this room already knows pain is hard. The question is whether it may be spoken plainly to God. And the Bible's answer will surprise anyone raised to think faith means never questioning, because Scripture wrote the sharpest version of the problem of pain into its own pages. His name is Job.

Job loses his children, his wealth, and his health. His wife tells him, "Curse God and die" (Job 2:9). The reader is let in on something Job never learns: there's no sin behind it, no lesson he failed. His friends insist that suffering must be deserved and that if he'd repent the pain would lift. Job refuses. For chapter after chapter he protests and demands a hearing, and in one sentence he holds both his trust and his protest: "Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face" (Job 13:15).

The atheist's case should be heard here at its strongest, because it isn't a cartoon. A world with this much undeserved agony, suffering that teaches nothing and falls on the innocent, is hard to square with a God who is perfectly good and fully able to stop it. If he can and won't, is he good? If he would and can't, is he God? That's one of the oldest and most serious questions a person can ask, and a faith that won't take it seriously isn't worth having.

The book of Job takes it seriously too. When God finally speaks, his anger falls not on Job but on the friends who explained: "you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7). God preferred the man who argued with him to the men who explained him.

But the atheist's case, real as its weight is, proves less than it claims. It assumes that a problem we can't solve means no one is there. In Job, the suffering that looked like an argument against God becomes the place where Job meets him. God answers out of the whirlwind, and what's astonishing is what the answer isn't. It isn't an explanation. God never tells Job about the scene in heaven. He gives Job himself: chapter after chapter of the one who "laid the foundation of the earth" (Job 38:4). And Job, who had demanded answers, says, "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you" (Job 42:5). He goes quiet, not because he was bullied but because he was met.

Most of us have been the friend more often than we've been Job. We've sat beside real grief and reached for the sentence that made us more comfortable and the other person more alone. The urge to answer is usually the urge to flee. And the gospel under this whole study is that God did the opposite of what we keep doing. He didn't send an explanation into the world's suffering. He came into it himself. He stood at a grave he was about to open, and before he opened it, he wept.

scriptureStudy.note: "The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Job's first response is worship, before he understands anything. The book won't let this be his last word, but it doesn't treat it as nothing.
"Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire?" The same man who worshiped now wishes he'd never lived. Scripture puts both on the page.
"Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face." Job won't let go of God and won't pretend he's fine, and the Bible calls that faith.

"Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" God's answer begins with questions Job can't answer. It moves Job from the center of the universe to a creature before his Maker, and somehow that is the comfort.
"I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you." Job never gets his explanation. He gets an encounter, and it's enough.
"You have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has." God rebukes the friends who defended him with tidy theology and vindicates the man who protested.
"In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider: God has made the one as well as the other." The Preacher refuses to read prosperity as reward and adversity as punishment.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at the history of the question. The word theodicy, an attempt to justify God in the face of evil, comes from the philosopher Gottfried Leibniz, whose book by that name appeared in 1710 and argued that ours is the best of all possible worlds. On November 1, 1755, All Saints' Day, an earthquake destroyed Lisbon while many people were at church. Voltaire answered Leibniz's optimism with a poem on the disaster and then with the satire Candide. Both men were trying to solve suffering like an equation, one way or the other. The book of Job had refused that equation long before.

Then set two books by C. S. Lewis side by side. In The Problem of Pain (1940) he argued carefully for God in the face of suffering, including his well-known image of pain as God's megaphone. After his wife died, he wrote A Grief Observed (1961), which at times reads like an argument with the earlier book. Ask the group what that pairing shows: an answer that satisfies in a study can shatter at a graveside. And watch that your group doesn't turn suffering into a puzzle to solve while the person in pain among you feels more alone.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group is the fixer, the one who can't stand an unresolved problem. When another member shares a raw, unanswered grief, he immediately offers reasons: God is working this for good, there must be a purpose, at least it wasn't worse. He isn't cruel. He believes answers are love.

Honor him before you correct him; his wish to help is real. But notice what his answers are doing. Each one closes a door the grieving person needed left open, and lands as a quiet instruction to stop feeling what they feel. He's being Job's friend. Don't shame him in front of the room, because most of us have done the same. Afterward, ask him gently whether his answers are for the sufferer's comfort or his own.

Use this to show the difference between fixing a pain and bearing it with someone. Ask the group which they've more often been given, and which they've more often given.

sessions.title: Permission to Complain to God
sessions.aim: To recover lament as faithful speech rather than a lapse of faith, to see that about a third of the Psalms teach God's people to bring grief and protest straight to him, and to refuse the forced brightness that drives honest sorrow underground.
sessions.summary:
For many people, Sunday morning is a hard hour. A room full of people carrying real griefs agrees to sing as though none of them were there. The singing isn't wrong. But many churches have quietly taught that faith sounds only one way, upbeat and resolved, and that sorrow brought into worship is a kind of failure.

What does the Bible actually give us to pray when life caves in? About a third of the Psalms are laments: "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Psalm 22:1). These are Scripture, put in our mouths on purpose.

There is such a thing as corrosive complaint, and the session names the difference between lament and grumbling. But a smile that won't admit the wound isn't trust either; often it's fear that God can't handle the truth about us. The laments usually turn toward God's faithfulness, and they turn only after the complaint has been said in full. You get to trust through the sorrow, not around it.

keyScripture.why: "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?" (Psalm 13:1). The psalmist accuses God to his face and keeps addressing him, and this complaint is part of Scripture's own prayer book.

discussion.q: Where have you felt you had to hide your grief in church to seem faithful?
discussion.behind: Start gently. Many people carry an unspoken rule that a good Christian is always fine. Let the room name the gap between the face they bring and what they carry in.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 13 and Psalm 22:1-2. What does it change to know that words like these are Scripture, not faithlessness?
discussion.behind: Most people have never been told the Bible's prayer book is full of protest. God didn't just tolerate these prayers; he gave them to us to pray.

discussion.q: Scripture warns against grumbling (Philippians 2:14). Where's the line between faithful lament and grumbling?
discussion.behind: Keep this fair. The clue is direction. Lament speaks to God and keeps holding on; grumbling speaks about God, to others, and slowly lets go. Don't let the line become a way to shame people back into silence. In most churches the danger is too little lament, not too much.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 42:9-11. The psalmist complains and tells himself to hope in the same breath. Why do you think the turn comes through the sorrow and not around it?
discussion.behind: Nothing outside the psalmist changes. He reaches hope because he was first allowed to say the whole thing. Don't rush the turn.

discussion.q: Where has a brightness you show God been protecting you from telling him the truth?
discussion.behind: Go first. Many of us offer God a managed version of ourselves out of fear. Hiding from God isn't reverence; it's distance.

objections.objection: The Bible tells us to give thanks in all circumstances and to rejoice always. All this permission to complain just baptizes self-pity.
objections.response: Those commands are real (1 Thessalonians 5:18; Philippians 4:4), and a life of endless grievance is a real spiritual danger. Gratitude is healthier than a permanent grudge. But the same Bible gives us a prayer book full of laments, so these must be held together, not set against each other. The difference isn't between complaint and gratitude. It's between grumbling and lament. Grumbling talks about God to other people and lets go of him. Lament talks to God, holds on, and usually turns toward his faithfulness. Self-pity ends in the self. Lament ends in God.

objections.objection: If I really trusted God, I wouldn't need to complain to him. Bringing him my anger shows my faith is weak. I should accept his will without protest.
objections.response: There's real reverence in that, and it's trying to honor God. But if bringing God your anguish showed weak faith, then Job, the psalmists, Jeremiah, and Jesus himself, who prayed Psalm 22 from the cross, all had weak faith, and that can't be right. It takes more faith to bring God your fury than to bury it, because burying it assumes he can't be trusted with the real you. Accepting God's will is good. It's where the lament psalms are headed, not a shortcut that skips the truth-telling.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What grief or anger have you been bringing to everyone except God? What would it mean to say all of it to him this week?
sessions.practice: This week, pray a lament psalm as your own, slowly, out loud if you can: Psalm 13, Psalm 22, or Psalm 88. Let the words carry the grief you haven't known how to say, including the parts that accuse. Don't skip to the turn at the end until you've meant the complaint at the beginning. If your own lament runs longer than the psalm, keep going in your own words, but keep talking to God. Write down what happened in you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, we've brought you our best manners and hidden our worst grief, as though you were a guest to impress instead of a Father who already sees. Forgive the brightness we mistook for trust. Forgive us for teaching each other that faith may only sound one way, and for the sorrow we've driven underground. Thank you that you wrote our complaints into your own book and put them in our mouths. Teach us to say the whole hard thing to you and keep holding on, and to find, on the far side of it, that you were faithful all along. Where a sorrow has grown too heavy to carry alone, give us courage to let another person in. Amen.
reflection: Where have I shown a settled faith I didn't feel, and what has that cost me?
Do I know, in my own heart, the difference between lament that holds on to God and grumbling that lets go?
What would change if I believed God would rather have my angry, truthful prayer than my polite, distant one?
sessions.teaching:
For a lot of people, Sunday morning is the hardest hour of the week. A room full of people carrying heavy griefs quietly agrees to sing as though none of those griefs were in the building. I want to be careful here. The singing isn't the problem, and the joy isn't fake in everyone. But over generations many churches have taught a lie about what faith sounds like: upbeat, resolved, grateful, settled. Sorrow brought into worship feels like a leak. So people learn to leave their grief in the car and answer "fine."

Underneath that is a simple question the church has strangely forgotten how to answer. What does the Bible actually give us to pray when life caves in? Not what we should feel, or how fast we should recover, but what words God himself puts in our mouths for the day the diagnosis comes, or the marriage ends, or the prayer is met with silence.

The answer is lament. About a third of the Psalms are laments: complaints, grief, and confusion from people who kept talking to God at the very moments they were most upset with him. "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Psalm 22:1). "I say to God, my rock: 'Why have you forgotten me?'" (Psalm 42:9). These aren't prayers that needed correcting. They're Scripture, which means the sorrow you were taught to hide has a voice in the Bible waiting for you.

The other side has a point. There's a corrosive kind of complaint. Some people take a real wound and build their whole identity around it, or use their pain as a standing excuse to be unkind. Paul tells the church to "Do all things without grumbling" (Philippians 2:14), and a grateful heart really is healthier than a bitter one.

But the difference that matters isn't between complaint and gratitude. It's between grumbling and lament, and they aren't the same thing. Grumbling talks about God to other people and slowly lets go of him. Lament talks to God and holds on. And the fixed smile that many churches offer instead isn't the opposite of grumbling. Most of the time it isn't trust at all. It's fear: the worry that if God saw the real anger and doubt, he'd turn away. So we show him only the parts we think he can stand, and we call that reverence. It's really distance.

Here's what the laments teach. They almost always turn. Psalm 13 begins with "How long?" and ends, "I will sing to the LORD, because he has dealt bountifully with me" (Psalm 13:6). But look at how the turn comes. Nothing outside the psalmist changes between the first verse and the last. The turn comes by remembering the God the complaint is addressed to, and it comes only after the complaint has been said in full. Psalm 42 shows it happening in real time: "Why are you cast down, O my soul ... Hope in God; for I shall again praise him" (Psalm 42:11). You can't reach trust by suppressing grief. You get there through it.

And the darkest lament, Psalm 88, doesn't turn at all. It ends in darkness, and God left it in the book anyway, which tells us that even a prayer that finds no light is still a prayer he hears. So we're invited to a harder kind of honesty than Sunday morning usually allows: to say the whole thing to the God who wrote the words for us, and to trust, not that the pain will be quickly explained, but that the one who gave us these prayers is strong enough and near enough to hear them.

scriptureStudy.note: "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?" Four accusations and no apology, and God put it in the songbook.
"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" The cry Jesus takes up on the cross begins here, in a lament. The sinless Son prayed the language of protest.
"You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness." This lament never turns, and God kept it anyway.
"Why have you forgotten me?" and then, "Hope in God; for I shall again praise him." The complaint and the call to hope sit in the same breath.
"Remember my affliction and my wanderings, the wormwood and the gall!" then, "But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope." Hope is remembered inside the grief, not instead of it.
"O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear?" A prophet opens his book by telling God he isn't listening, and the book is Scripture.
"My soul is very sorrowful, even to death." In Gethsemane Jesus doesn't perform calm. He names his sorrow at its full weight.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, read the Old Testament scholar Walter Brueggemann on the Psalms. He describes them as moving between orientation, disorientation, and new orientation, and in a 1986 essay, "The Costly Loss of Lament," he argued that a church that drops lament from its worship leaves its people with no sanctioned words for their pain. Take his diagnosis seriously, and notice that the cure he points to is old, not new: the Bible's own neglected songs.

Then read Nicholas Wolterstorff's Lament for a Son (1987), written after his twenty-five-year-old son died in a climbing accident. It refuses every comfort that would make the death smaller. Ask the group: if about a third of the Psalms are laments, is a church that can't lament more faithful than the Bible, or less? What would it take for your church to treat lament as a normal part of faith?
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group lost a pregnancy several months ago and, by every outward sign, is doing beautifully: serving, smiling, quick to say God is good and she's at peace. When this session names the brightness that hides a wound, she goes quiet. Then she says carefully that she hasn't cried since it happened, because she was afraid grieving would mean she didn't trust God.

Be tender and unhurried. Don't treat her peace as fake; some of it may be real. Don't pull the scab off in front of the room. Gently give back what she's been missing: permission to grieve without it counting against her faith. The psalmists wept and asked why. Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb knowing he'd raise him. Offer her a lament psalm to pray this week and a private conversation if she wants one.

Use this to show the group that composure isn't the goal. Honesty with God is.
