sessions.title: A God Who Does Not Explain, but Comes
sessions.aim: To see that God's final response to suffering is not an argument but his own participation in it: at the cross God enters the world's godforsakenness instead of accounting for it from a distance. And to refuse both the picture of a God untouched above pain and the despair that reads pain as proof he's absent.
sessions.summary:
Many skeptics assume that if there were a God, he'd stay above the mess, serene and untouched, explaining the world's agony from a distance or ignoring it. The Christian claim is stranger. Ask where God was when it hurt, and Christianity's answer is a place. He was on a cross, crying out the first line of a lament: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34).

The German theologian Jürgen Moltmann, who began to come to faith as a prisoner of war after the Second World War, wrote The Crucified God (1972) arguing that God isn't a spectator of human suffering but took it into himself at the cross, so there's no depth of abandonment where God hasn't been.

There's a serious objection: a God who suffers sounds weak, and Christian thinkers long insisted God can't be overwhelmed. That concern guards something true. But the cross doesn't explain suffering. It means that when you go down into the dark, you don't go where God has never been. He went first, and the marks are on his hands.

keyScripture.why: "And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, 'Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?' which means, 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?'" (Mark 15:34). God the Son enters human godforsakenness and prays a lament from inside it.

discussion.q: What have you assumed God does with human suffering? Where did that picture come from?
discussion.behind: Bring out the working picture, not the doctrine. Many people quietly imagine a distant, unbothered God. The gap between that picture and the cross is where this session lives.

discussion.q: Read Mark 15:33-39. What does it mean to you that God himself has prayed the prayer of the forsaken?
discussion.behind: Jesus doesn't float serenely through his death. He enters abandonment and prays Psalm 22. There's no place of godforsakenness people in your room can reach that he hasn't entered.

discussion.q: What changes when the answer to your suffering isn't an explanation but a God who entered it?
discussion.behind: It solves less on paper and comforts more in a hospital room. Keep it concrete.

discussion.q: Some Christians have worried that a God who suffers is a weak God. What's right about wanting a strong God? How does Philippians 2:6-8 hold strength and suffering together?
discussion.behind: Keep both. The church has rightly insisted that God isn't overwhelmed by evil. Philippians shows the Son choosing to go down, "obedient to the point of death" (Philippians 2:8). Love by its nature is willing to be wounded.

discussion.q: Where in your own pain would it change things to know God had been there before you?
discussion.behind: Go first if the room is slow. Invite people to name a specific dark they've walked through. End in presence, not a tidy resolution.

objections.objection: A God who suffers and cries out in abandonment is a weak, human-sized God. The point of God is that he's above all that. A wounded God needs saving as much as we do.
objections.response: That instinct is ancient and serious. Christian thinkers who insisted that God can't be overwhelmed or changed by the world were guarding something true: God isn't a bigger version of us, buffeted and needy, and a god who was only a cosmic victim couldn't save anyone. But the cross doesn't show a God overwhelmed against his will. It shows the Son freely choosing to enter the place his creatures most needed him, without ceasing to be God. He "emptied himself" and became "obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross" (Philippians 2:7-8). That's strength that can afford to be wounded. And love that risks nothing and can be moved by nothing isn't love. A God safely above the mess would be tidy on paper and no help in a hospital room.

objections.objection: Even if God suffered on the cross, that was one afternoon two thousand years ago. It does nothing about my suffering today.
objections.response: The distance you feel is real, and nobody should be handed a doctrine when they need a presence. But the cross isn't only a past event to admire. It shows who God is: the God whose love enters instead of avoiding. Scripture says "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted" (Psalm 34:18). That describes his settled character, shown at the cross, and true in the dark places since. This doesn't remove your pain. It changes whether you suffer alone in a place God avoids, or with him in a place he has already entered and enters still.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: In the darkest place your suffering has taken you, did God feel absent or present? How might the cross change the way you remember it?
sessions.practice: This week, take the specific dark you've known, the loss or fear or abandonment, and deliberately set the cross beside it in prayer. Don't try to explain your suffering, and don't ask the cross to explain it. Hold the two together and tell God that he's been in this place before you, that the cry of the forsaken was his cry too, and ask him to make his presence as real as his absence has sometimes felt. Write down whether it changed how alone the pain felt.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, we expected a God who stayed above our suffering, safe and serene, and instead you came down into it and let it close over your head. You cried out the prayer of the forsaken so that no forsaken person would be alone in the dark again. Forgive us for wanting a God too strong to be wounded, when your wounds show how you love. Where we've felt abandoned, teach us that you were there before us and are there still. And for everyone here carrying a grief too heavy to name, come, not with an answer, but with yourself. Amen.
reflection: What picture of God do I actually carry into my suffering, and how does the cross correct it?
Have I wanted a God too strong to be wounded? What would it mean to trust the strength that chose the wounds?
Where have I felt most abandoned, and what would change if I believed God had already been in that exact place?
sessions.teaching:
For many people who don't believe, the cross means very little. It's religious furniture, a symbol other people find moving. That's because unbelief quietly assumes something about God: if he existed, he'd stay above the mess. Serene, complete, untouched, running the universe from a safe distance, either explaining its agony with a plan too high for us or simply not bothered by it. On that assumption the problem of pain really is unanswerable. A God who could stop your child's suffering and only watches from his height would be a monster.

So this session asks the oldest and most personal question a sufferer asks: where was God when it hurt? Not in the abstract, but when the phone rang, when the room went silent, when the prayer came back empty. And Christianity's answer isn't a theory. It's a place. He was on a cross, in the dark at noon, crying out, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34). He entered the very godforsakenness the problem of pain is made of.

The German theologian Jürgen Moltmann is worth knowing here, because he didn't learn this in a library. He was a young soldier when he was taken prisoner in 1945, and he spent the next three years in prisoner-of-war camps as the full horror of what his nation had done became known. A chaplain gave him a New Testament with the Psalms, and there he began to come to faith. In 1972 he published The Crucified God. His argument is that God isn't the unmoved spectator of the world's agony; at the cross God took human suffering into himself, so there's no depth of abandonment where God hasn't been. He draws on a scene from Elie Wiesel's memoir Night: a boy hanged in a death camp while the prisoners are forced to watch, and a man behind Wiesel asking where God is now. Wiesel wasn't making a Christian point. Moltmann reads the scene in the light of the cross, as God present with the godforsaken.

There's a serious case on the other side, and it has a long history in the church. Many Christian thinkers held that God in his divine nature can't suffer or change, because suffering implies need and God lacks nothing. A God who suffers, the objection runs, is a weak God who needs rescuing as much as we do. There's a real truth there: God isn't just a bigger, sadder version of us.

But the cross doesn't show God overwhelmed against his will. Paul says the Son, "though he was in the form of God," "emptied himself" and became "obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross" (Philippians 2:6-8). That's the God of all power choosing to go down to the place his creatures most needed him, without ceasing for a moment to be God. Isaiah had already said of Israel's God, "In all their affliction he was afflicted" (Isaiah 63:9). And it shows what a God who couldn't be touched could never do. Love that risks nothing and can be moved by nothing isn't love. Love is always willing to be wounded.

I need to be clear about what this does and doesn't do. It doesn't explain suffering. If you came hoping the cross would finally give you the reason your grief has been demanding, it won't. What it does is harder and, in a hospital room, better. When you go down into the dark, you don't go where God has never been. He went first. And by his Spirit he's in the dark with you now, not as the memory of an execution long ago but because that's who he is.

There's a kind of suffering no explanation would touch even if you had one. The only thing that helps is not being alone in it. And the gospel's deepest word to the sufferer isn't "here is why." It's "I am here." The marks are on his hands. He's been where you are, and he didn't leave.

scriptureStudy.note: "He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief." The servant of the LORD knows grief from the inside.
"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" God the Son prays a lament from within real abandonment, so the cry of the forsaken has been God's own cry.
"Jesus wept." Moments before raising his friend, he grieves. God doesn't stand above our sorrow explaining it.
"We do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses." The one we come to in suffering has felt it.
"Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered." Scripture isn't embarrassed to say the incarnate Son was shaped by suffering.

"Though he was in the form of God ... he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross." God's movement is downward, and Scripture calls that descent glory, not weakness.
"In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them." Long before the cross, God is described as present in his people's suffering.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, take up the old question of whether God can suffer, and don't settle it in a sentence. The classical tradition, running through Augustine and Aquinas, taught divine impassibility: God in his divine nature isn't subject to suffering or change. That wasn't carelessness. It guarded God's perfection and freedom and kept him from being a needy being at the mercy of the world. In the twentieth century, Moltmann's The Crucified God (1972) challenged it, arguing that the cross shows God truly entering suffering.

Both sides are protecting something real: God isn't overwhelmed by evil, and in Christ he really did enter pain. Many careful theologians hold both: God doesn't suffer as we do, helplessly and against his will, yet in Christ he freely takes suffering into himself out of love. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from a Nazi prison in 1944, put it in one line: only a suffering God can help (paraphrased; Letters and Papers from Prison). Then bring the discussion back under Scripture, which gives us not a theory but a story: a God who weeps at a tomb, is afflicted in his people's affliction, and cries out forsaken from a cross.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group has been circling the edges of faith for months. He says plainly that what keeps him from believing is the suffering he's seen, a friend's long death from cancer, and he can't worship a God who would allow it. He isn't being provocative. He's telling the truth.

Don't rush to defend God, and don't treat his unbelief as a problem to fix in one evening. Agree that a God who watched his friend die from an untroubled distance would deserve to be rejected. Then, gently, offer him not an argument but the strange fact at the center of the faith: the God he's rejecting isn't that spectator. He entered suffering himself and cried out forsaken. Don't press for a decision.

Use this to show the group how to answer a hard objection without winning an argument. If he leaves still unconvinced, he should at least leave unable to say that believing means pretending suffering doesn't matter.

memoryVerse.text: For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.

sessions.title: The Thorn That Was Not Removed
sessions.aim: To take seriously the slow work suffering can do, the endurance, character, and hope Paul names, without turning it into a formula that makes pain a tidy means to a good end, and to sit with the prayer God answered by not removing the thorn.
sessions.summary:
Romans 8:28 is one of the most misused verses in a hospital room. "For those who love God all things work together for good" isn't false. The trouble is how fast we say it and to whom. Wrestled toward over years by the one who suffers, it's hard-won faith. Offered by a bystander in the first raw week, it's a lid on a grief.

Paul says something careful: "suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope" (Romans 5:3-4). It isn't a promise that every pain pays off on schedule. And look who says it: a man beaten, shipwrecked, imprisoned, and left with a "thorn ... in the flesh" he begged God three times to remove. God said no: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9).

Some pain produces nothing but ruin, and talk of character over a child's grave is obscene. But saying suffering produces good is a formula and a lie. Saying God can bring good out of suffering is the testimony of people who have been through it.

keyScripture.why: "But he said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness'" (2 Corinthians 12:9). God answers Paul's prayer for relief without removing the thorn or explaining it. He promises grace that is enough.

discussion.q: Have you been on either end of Romans 8:28, saying it or hearing it? How did it land?
discussion.behind: Don't let anyone leave thinking the verse is false; it's deeply true. The same words can be faith when won and cruelty when imposed. Timing and who's speaking make the difference.

discussion.q: Read 2 Corinthians 11:23-28 and 12:7-10. Why does it matter that the man who wrote Romans 5:3-5 was himself denied relief?
discussion.behind: Paul isn't theorizing from comfort. That's the only place such a claim can be made without becoming an insult.

discussion.q: What's the difference between saying "suffering produces good" and "God can bring good out of suffering"?
discussion.behind: Grant fully that suffering often destroys, and that saying otherwise over a fresh grave is cruel. Then draw the line: the first is a formula; the second is testimony, usually spoken later, by the person who suffered.

discussion.q: Have you ever received a "no" from God that came with grace instead of an explanation?
discussion.behind: Many have prayed for something to be taken away and watched it stay. For some the thorn is still fresh and the grace not yet felt. Don't force a triumphant reading.

discussion.q: Where are you still asking God to remove a thorn? What would it mean to ask also for grace that's enough while it stays?
discussion.behind: Go first, and offer this as an invitation, not a command. It's a costly prayer that can't be demanded of someone still bleeding.

objections.objection: Telling people their suffering is producing character is offensive when they're living through the worst thing that ever happened to them. Plenty of suffering just destroys people.
objections.response: That's largely true, and failing to say so has wounded many grieving people. Suffering doesn't automatically produce anything good. It often produces bitterness and breakdown, and talking about character over a fresh grave isn't comfort. Scripture never asks us to say it. But there's a line the objection blurs. Saying suffering produces good is a formula, and it's false. Saying God can bring good out of suffering is the testimony of people who have walked through the dark and come out still holding on. Paul never says the thorn was good. He says God's grace was sufficient in it. That's a hope people discover from the inside, usually long after, never on command.

objections.objection: If God could have removed Paul's thorn and chose not to, then God lets people suffer when he could stop it. That's the whole problem again.
objections.response: It is the problem of pain in a sharper, more personal form, and it shouldn't be dodged. God could have removed the thorn. He said no. But his no wasn't silence or indifference. It was a promise of his own grace and power in the very place of Paul's weakness. Paul asked for the thorn gone and was given God's presence in it, and he concluded, "when I am weak, then I am strong" (2 Corinthians 12:10). This doesn't answer why God permits suffering, and the study won't pretend it does. It shows that God's no isn't always abandonment.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What thorn have you asked God three times, or three hundred, to remove? Could you also begin to ask for grace that's enough to bear it, or is that prayer still too costly?
sessions.practice: This week, take the thorn you keep asking God to remove and change one prayer. Keep asking for relief if you need to, but add the harder prayer beside it: that his grace would be enough while the thorn remains, and that his strength would show up in your weakness. Watch for grace that comes not as rescue but as enough. Write down whether it changed how you carried it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we've prayed for the thorn to be taken, again and again. Sometimes you've taken it, and sometimes you've said what you said to Paul: your grace is enough, and your power is made perfect in our weakness. Forgive us the times we turned suffering into a formula and told the grieving their pain was making them better, when what they needed was our silence and our tears. Teach us the difference between the lie that suffering produces good and the hope that you can bring good out of it. Where the thorn remains, give us grace to bear it. And where a burden has grown too heavy, send us people to help carry it, and make us those people for someone else. Amen.
reflection: Where have I told myself or others that pain automatically produces growth?
Have I only asked God to remove my thorn, or also for grace to bear it? What does my reluctance tell me?
What would it mean to believe God's strength is made perfect in my weakness, not by finally making me strong enough to need no grace?
sessions.teaching:
Romans 8:28 may be the most misused verse in a hospital room: "And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose." I want to be careful, because the verse isn't false. It's true, and it has held up more grieving believers than anyone could count. The problem is how fast we say it and to whom. From someone who has fought her way toward it over years in the dark, it's one of the hardest-won sentences in Scripture. From a bystander in the first raw week of someone else's grief, the same words become a lid on a wound that's still trying to breathe.

So this session asks what suffering actually does, and whether we can say anything true about it without turning pain into a machine that manufactures growth. There's a version of Christian teaching that treats every hardship as an investment guaranteed to pay a spiritual dividend. That version isn't only false. It's cruel, and it has driven wounded people out of the church.

Paul speaks more carefully than we do. He writes, "we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame" (Romans 5:3-5). It's a real sequence, and I'm not going to explain it away. But it isn't a promise that every pain pays off on a timetable you can hold God to. It describes what God can grow in a life that stays with him.

And look at who's saying it. Paul tells the Corinthians, "Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked" (2 Corinthians 11:24-25). On top of that he carried "a thorn ... in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me" (2 Corinthians 12:7). We're never told what it was, and it doesn't matter. What matters is that it didn't lift. "Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me" (2 Corinthians 12:8). God didn't say it would make sense later. He didn't give a reason. He didn't say yes. "But he said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness'" (2 Corinthians 12:9).

The case against all this needs to be heard, and anyone who has stood near a grave can feel it. Talk of suffering producing endurance and character isn't just unhelpful at a child's funeral; it's obscene. Some suffering produces nothing but ruin. It breaks people and doesn't build them. That's often simply true, and refusing to admit it is what has made the formula so hateful. To tell a devastated parent their loss is building their character is to sin against them with a Bible verse.

But here's the line the objection blurs, and the session hangs on it. Saying suffering produces good is a formula, and it's a lie. Saying God can bring good out of suffering isn't a formula at all. It's the testimony of people who have gone down into the worst of it and come out still holding on to God, and it can only be said from the inside, usually looking back, by the one who suffered. It can never be imposed from outside on someone still bleeding. Paul never says the thorn was good. He says God's grace was sufficient in it.

So the deepest gift God gives a sufferer is often not the thorn removed. It's his presence given in its place, and a strange strength that shows up exactly where you're weakest and stop pretending to be strong. Paul ends somewhere that sounds like madness until you've been there: "For when I am weak, then I am strong" (2 Corinthians 12:10). That isn't positive thinking, and it isn't the thorn made pretty. It's a man who asked for rescue, received God's presence instead, and found that the presence was worth more. Most of us will spend years asking God to remove the thorn. The harder prayer, the one Paul was driven to, is to ask for grace that's enough while it stays.

scriptureStudy.note: "Suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope." A real sequence, not a formula, written by a man who knew unrelieved pain.
"A thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me." Scripture never names the thorn, which lets anyone with an affliction that won't lift find themselves in Paul's.

"Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this ... But he said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you.'" God answers a prayer for relief with grace, not removal or explanation. A no from God isn't the same as abandonment.

"For those who love God all things work together for good." Precious when won by a sufferer, cruel when slapped on a fresh grief. It promises not that suffering is good but that God can work good even through it.

"Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness." The joy is counted and chosen, aimed at maturity, not a pretense that the trial doesn't hurt.
"Though now for a little while, if necessary, you have been grieved by various trials." Peter gives the grief its full weight before he speaks of what the testing refines.
"Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day." Wasting and renewing in one sentence: the decay isn't denied, and it isn't the last word.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at the narrow ground between denying that suffering can form us and claiming it automatically improves us. Timothy Keller's Walking with God through Pain and Suffering (2013) is a careful guide. Weigh it against prosperity teaching, which promises that suffering will be brief and productive if you have enough faith. This study names that teaching as false.

Older Christians often spoke of affliction as a school. Notice how easily that language turns into a formula when it's spoken over someone else's grief instead of out of one's own. Psychologists also describe what they call post-traumatic growth: some people come out of severe suffering with deeper relationships and clearer priorities. Grant what's true in that. Then name what it can't promise: growth isn't guaranteed, much trauma produces only wreckage, and the finding is no comfort to offer someone freshly bereaved. The Christian claim is different. God can bring good out of what he didn't send, on a timeline he doesn't disclose, by a grace the sufferer receives rather than manufactures.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group lives with chronic pain that no treatment has relieved. For years, kind believers have told her that God must be building something in her, that there's a purpose, that she'll understand one day. She's worn out by it, and she comes into this session braced for more.

Refuse the formula before you offer anything. Don't tell her what her suffering is producing; you aren't living in her body. Say plainly that her pain may not produce anything she can point to, and that the people who kept explaining it were wrong to. Then, without pressing, mention that Paul was denied relief too, his thorn stayed, and he wasn't told why. His answer from God wasn't removal or explanation but grace and presence in it. Don't require her to feel that grace on cue.

Use this to show the group that the gift isn't another explanation. It's ending the demand that she produce one, and staying with her in the pain.

memoryVerse.text: But he said to me, "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness."

sessions.title: Every Tear, and Whose Hand Wipes It
sessions.aim: To set all suffering under the promise of the new creation, where God himself wipes away every tear, to see present suffering as real but not final, and to refuse both the sentimentality that skips to the ending and the despair that can't believe there is one.
sessions.summary:
There are two cheap things to do with Christian hope: grab it too early, and give it up. Grief is tempted toward both. This session asks whether the suffering we've refused to explain gets the last word. The answer at the heart of the faith is no, but it's not a no that comes cheaply.

The Bible doesn't end with souls escaping to a cloud. It ends with heaven coming down, God dwelling with his people, and a sentence that has been read at countless gravesides: "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away" (Revelation 21:4). God does the wiping himself.

The skeptic will call this wishful thinking, and the suspicion deserves to be heard. But the Christian hope rests on an empty tomb, not on how much we need it. Dietrich Bonhoeffer called the things before God's final word the penultimate, the next-to-last. Present suffering is real, and it's next-to-last. A last word is coming.

keyScripture.why: "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more" (Revelation 21:4). The last word over all suffering, spoken by God himself bending to every grieving face.

discussion.q: Which are you more tempted toward: grabbing hope too early and skipping your grief, or giving hope up entirely? Why?
discussion.behind: Grabbing it early is sentimentality; giving it up is despair. Both avoid the hard middle where the pain and the hope are both real.

discussion.q: Read Revelation 21:1-5. The Bible ends with heaven coming down, not with us escaping. What changes when the hope is this world healed rather than left behind?
discussion.behind: Many imagine floating off to a cloud. The biblical hope is a new creation with embodied people and God dwelling with them. It takes present grief seriously because what was lost will be restored, not discarded.

discussion.q: God himself, not an angel, wipes away the tears. What does that mean to you?
discussion.behind: Let the tenderness land. The God who wept at Lazarus's tomb is the one who dries each face at the end.

discussion.q: Some say heaven is a comfort people invented because life is unbearable without it. What's true in that suspicion? Read 1 Corinthians 15:14-20. Where does Paul rest the hope?
discussion.behind: Be fair to the skeptic. A comfort could be invented because it's needed. Paul rests everything on whether Christ was raised, and admits that if he wasn't, "your faith is futile."

discussion.q: How would it change the way you carry your pain to hold it as real and as not the final word, both at once?
discussion.behind: End the study here, with weight and hope, not a tidy bow. Watch for anyone whose grief has turned to despair, and follow the care note in the leader's guide.

objections.objection: The promise that God will wipe away every tear is obviously wishful thinking. People invented heaven because life is unbearable without believing in something better.
objections.response: That suspicion is fair, and a hope that can't face it isn't worth holding. A comfort can be invented because it's needed. But needing something doesn't make it false; hunger doesn't prove there's no bread. And Christianity doesn't finally rest its hope on our need. It rests it on a claim about an event: that a man who was dead was raised, and the tomb was empty. Paul stakes everything on it: "if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile" (1 Corinthians 15:17). You can dispute that claim, and serious people do. But it's a claim about something that either happened or didn't, not a wish dressed up as fact.

objections.objection: A future where every tear is wiped away does nothing about the tears now. Promising a happy ending someday is a way of getting people to accept suffering instead of doing something about it.
objections.response: The church has sometimes deserved that charge. A future hope can be misused to excuse indifference now, and that's a sin. But held rightly, the hope does the opposite. The God who promises to wipe away every tear at the end is the God who entered suffering at the cross and tells his people to "weep with those who weep" (Romans 12:15) now. The new creation shows that present pain matters so much that God himself will undo it, which is why we take it seriously in the meantime. The hope doesn't remove the tears now. It changes whether they're the last word.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you picture God himself wiping the tears from your face, and from the face of the person you've grieved most, what rises in you? Is it hope, or a hope you're afraid to let yourself feel?
sessions.practice: This week, hold your present grief and Revelation 21:4 together on purpose, without letting either cancel the other. Name the tear you're still crying, without skipping to the ending. Then say over that same grief that it's real but not final, and that the hand that will wipe it away is God's own. Don't force the feeling of hope. Just hold the two truths together, the "not yet" and the "surely." Write down what that does to your grief.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we've spent these weeks refusing to explain suffering away, and we won't explain it away now, because it's real and you know it's real; you wept at a grave. But we won't give pain the last word either, because you've promised a last word of your own. You will wipe away every tear with your own hand, and death will be no more, and mourning and crying and pain will be gone. We believe it not only because we need it, though we do, but because the tomb was empty. Let the "not yet" keep us honest and the "surely" keep us from despair. For anyone here whose pain has grown too heavy, let this be the day they reach for help and aren't ashamed, and let us be the hands you send. Come, Lord Jesus, and until you do, keep us. Amen.
reflection: Am I more tempted to grab hope too early or to give it up? What would it mean to hold both grief and hope?
Does the promise that God himself will wipe away my tears feel real, or like a hope I'm afraid to believe? Why?
What would change if I held my present suffering as real but not the final word over my life?
sessions.teaching:
There are two cheap things a person can do with Christian hope, and grief is tempted toward both, sometimes in the same hour. One is to grab the hope too early, reaching past the grief for the happy ending before you've let yourself feel the loss. That produces the sentimentality that makes so much Christian talk about heaven unbearable to someone in pain. The other is to give hope up, deciding the wound is the whole truth and no ending is coming. That's despair. This study has tried for five weeks to stand between them, where the suffering is fully real and the hope is fully real, and neither cancels the other.

So does the suffering we've refused to explain get the last word? The answer at the center of the faith is no. But I won't let that no arrive cheaply.

Look at how the Bible ends, because it isn't what most people picture. It doesn't end with souls escaping this world for a disembodied heaven. It ends with heaven coming down: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God" (Revelation 21:3). Then comes a sentence that has been read at more gravesides than almost any other: "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away" (Revelation 21:4).

Read it slowly. Every tear, not most. And death itself, the last enemy, not managed or explained but abolished. Isaiah saw the same end centuries earlier: "He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces" (Isaiah 25:8). And notice whose hand does it. Not an angel sent for the job. God himself, bending down to every face. The God who wept at Lazarus's tomb is the God who dries every tear at the end.

The skeptic's case deserves to be heard, because a hope that can't survive the question isn't worth having. People invented heaven, the argument goes, because life is unbearable without it, and the more consoling the promise, the more we should suspect we made it up. There's weight in that. A comfort can be invented because it's needed. But needing something doesn't make it false. Hunger doesn't prove there's no bread. And Christianity doesn't rest its hope on how much we need it. It rests it somewhere far more exposed: on a tomb found empty on a Sunday morning, on the claim that a man truly dead was truly raised. Paul says so plainly: "if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins" (1 Corinthians 15:17). Christians don't believe every tear will be wiped away because the world is unbearable otherwise. They believe it because they believe a grave came open, and the God who opened it can be trusted with the ending he has promised.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer gave the church a useful word for this. In his Ethics he distinguished the ultimate, God's final word, from the penultimate, the next-to-last things that fill the time before it. Present suffering is penultimate. That doesn't mean unreal. I've spent every session refusing the cheap answer and the forced smile and the formula that turns grief into growth. The pain is real, and it hurts exactly as much as it hurts. But it isn't the last word. Paul calls the whole creation's suffering "the pains of childbirth" (Romans 8:22): real pain, headed somewhere.

There is a last word coming, and it won't be spoken by death or disease or abandonment. It will be spoken by the God who bends down to dry the face of everyone who ever wept. Not yet. That's the honest part, and it's why we still grieve and why the tears are still allowed. But surely. That's why, as Paul says, we don't grieve "as others do who have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). We grieve and hope at the same time, holding the wound and the promise in one hand, until the day the hand that was pierced wipes the last tear away.

scriptureStudy.note: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man." The hope isn't our escape to God's place but God coming to ours, which is why the new creation honors this world and our bodies instead of discarding them.
"He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more." Every tear, and the hand that wipes them is God's own.
"He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces." Centuries before Revelation, Isaiah sees the same ending.
"The sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us." Paul doesn't say the sufferings are small. He says they'll be outweighed.
"The whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now." Present suffering as labor: real and painful, and headed toward a birth.
"The last enemy to be destroyed is death." Death is an enemy, and its destruction is promised, which is why grief is right and despair is not.
"That you may not grieve as others do who have no hope." Paul doesn't forbid grief. Christians still weep, but not as people for whom the tears are the final word.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at the shape of Christian hope, which is often misunderstood even inside the church. N. T. Wright's Surprised by Hope (2008) argues that the New Testament's hope isn't disembodied souls going to heaven but resurrection and new creation: the renewal of heaven and earth and the raising of the body. A hope like that takes the goodness of creation and the body seriously, and so takes the wrongness of suffering seriously too. Bonhoeffer's distinction between the ultimate and the penultimate, worked out in his Ethics, gives the group words for holding present suffering as real without letting it be final.

Then take up the hardest pastoral question, with care. The hope of the new creation must never be used as a weapon against present grief, telling the bereaved to stop crying because it will all be fine someday. Be especially watchful, in a study on suffering, for anyone whose pain has moved toward despair that will not lift or toward wanting to be gone. Make sure that person is met not with a verse alone but with real help: a pastor, a counselor, a doctor, a crisis line (in the US, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline), and the plain assurance that reaching for that help is not a failure of faith but an act of it.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group lost his wife two years ago. In his own words, he has made a kind of peace with never being happy again. He doesn't present it as a crisis; to him it's realism. When the session turns to the new creation, he says quietly that he finds it hard to believe and isn't sure he wants to, because hoping again feels like betraying his grief, or setting himself up to be crushed a second time.

Be gentle, unhurried, and watchful. Don't argue him into hope; his love for his wife is real and his sorrow is real. Agree that hoping again is frightening, and that his fear of betraying her memory comes from love. Then offer, carefully, that the hope of the new creation doesn't betray his grief. It honors it, because it says the wife he lost was so good that God himself will undo her loss. Hope doesn't require him to grieve less.

Be watchful, too. A settled hopelessness after a great loss can be closer to danger than it looks. If there's any sign his despair has turned toward not wanting to be here, meet it directly and kindly, make sure he isn't carrying it alone, connect him to a pastor or counselor without shaming him for needing one, and make sure he knows he can call or text 988 at any hour.

memoryVerse.text: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.

leaderPrimer:
A study on suffering can go wrong in two opposite directions, and you'll need to watch both. It can become a seminar, a room of people solving the problem of pain like an equation while the person who is actually suffering feels more alone with every clever point. Or it can collapse into a grief that circles without hope, where no one dares mention the resurrection. The aim is a room where the suffering and the hope are both fully real.

Set the tone the first night. This isn't a debate to win. It's a weight to carry together, and the person in the most pain sets the pace, not the person with the most to say. Name the cheap answers out loud early, everything happens for a reason, God needed another angel, at least it wasn't worse, so everyone knows this room doesn't run on them. When someone shares real grief, resist the urge to fix it, and help the room resist it too. The urge to explain someone's pain is usually the urge to escape it. Some of the best moments in these five weeks may have no words in them at all.

Now the part that isn't optional. In any group studying suffering, someone may be in acute grief, or in a despair that has grown dangerous, or quietly wondering whether they want to still be here. Watch for it. Before you begin, know how you'd respond, and have real resources ready: a pastor, a counselor, a doctor, a crisis line you can name and hand over (in the US, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline). If anyone signals that their pain has turned toward self-harm or toward not wanting to live, do not treat it as a discussion point and do not leave it to a verse. Meet it directly and kindly, stay with them, make sure they are not alone, and connect them to real help that day, and say plainly that reaching for that help is not a failure of faith but an act of it. Keep the path to help visible in every session, not just the last. You aren't a counselor, and nothing in this guide is medical advice.

Go in as a fellow sufferer, not as someone who has it all resolved. If you present yourself as the one with the answers, the room will perform a resolution it doesn't feel. Five weeks won't answer the problem of pain, and if you promise that, you'll fail. What five weeks can do is send a hurting person home less alone: knowing God permits the hard question, that lament is faithful speech, that at the cross he entered the dark first, that his grace can be enough in a thorn he doesn't remove, and that the last word over every tear is his own hand wiping it away.

faq.q: Is this study going to try to explain why God allows suffering?
faq.a: No, on purpose. It takes the problem of pain seriously and states the atheist's objection at its strongest, and then it declines to hand over a tidy explanation, because Scripture declines to. In Job, God never tells Job the reason. He gives Job himself, and Job, who had demanded answers, goes quiet because he was met. The study follows that lead. God's final response to pain wasn't a theory but the cross, where he entered the dark himself, and a promise, the new creation, where he wipes every tear away.

faq.q: What if someone in the group is in deep grief, or in a despair that has become dangerous?
faq.a: Take it seriously; in a study on suffering it's a real possibility. The leader primer urges every facilitator, before beginning, to know how they would respond and to have real resources ready, a pastor, a counselor, a physician, a crisis line that can be named and handed over (in the US, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline). Watch the room, especially the quiet person, and keep the path to help visible in every session. If anyone signals that their pain has turned toward self-harm or toward not wanting to live, do not treat it as a discussion point and do not answer it with a verse alone. Meet it directly and kindly, stay with them, make sure they are not alone, and connect them to real help that day, and say plainly that reaching for that help is not a failure of faith but an act of it. The God at the center of this study wept at a grave. He doesn't ask anyone to suffer alone, and neither should the group.

faq.q: Does the study say it's wrong to ask God why, or to be angry with him?
faq.a: The opposite. In Job, God rebuked the friends who explained and approved Job, who protested (Job 42:7). About a third of the Psalms are laments, and Jesus prayed the first line of one from the cross. What the study asks is that the question be aimed at God, not away from him. That's the difference between lament, which holds on, and grumbling, which lets go.

faq.q: Is this study going to be too heavy to sit through?
faq.a: It doesn't look away, but that isn't the same as depressing. It refuses to minimize suffering and refuses despair just as firmly. Every session ends in prayer, and the last one ends with the new creation, where God himself wipes away every tear. People in pain usually find honesty a relief, because many have been carrying grief in rooms with no place for it.

faq.q: What does the study mean when it says the cross is God's answer to suffering?
faq.a: That Christianity's deepest answer to "where was God when it hurt?" is a place: a cross. Drawing on Jürgen Moltmann's The Crucified God, the study says God didn't stay above suffering but entered it in Christ, who cried out the prayer of the forsaken. This doesn't explain suffering, and the study says so. It means that when you go into the dark, you don't go where God has never been.

faq.q: Does the study teach that suffering is good for us?
faq.a: No. It names that formula as false and often cruel. There's a world of difference between "suffering produces good," which is a lie, and "God can bring good out of suffering," which is the testimony of people who have come through it still holding on. Paul begged God three times to remove his thorn and was told, "My grace is sufficient for you" (2 Corinthians 12:9). The thorn wasn't good. The grace was enough.

faq.q: Is the hope of heaven in the last session just wishful thinking?
faq.a: The study takes that suspicion seriously. A comfort can be invented because it's needed. But needing something doesn't make it false, and Christianity rests its hope on a claim about an event, the resurrection of Jesus, not on our need. Paul says that if Christ wasn't raised, faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:17). You can dispute the claim; serious people do. But it's a claim about something that either happened or didn't.

faq.q: The study keeps refusing cheap answers. Does it have any answers at all?
faq.a: It has a great deal to say, but it won't say false things. It refuses the lines that ease the speaker's discomfort at the sufferer's expense, and the formula that turns pain into a growth program. What it offers is permission to bring the hard question to God, lament as faithful speech, the cross where God entered the dark, grace that's enough in the thorn that stays, and the promise that suffering isn't final. It simply won't pretend to have a neat explanation for any one person's pain.

faq.q: What does "penultimate" mean, and why does the study end on it?
faq.a: It means next-to-last. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, in his Ethics, distinguished the ultimate, God's final word, from the penultimate, the things that fill the time before it. Present suffering is penultimate: not unreal, but not final. The "not yet" is why we still grieve. The "surely" is why we don't grieve as those who have no hope.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't this just religion offering comfort it can't back up?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion. The study grants that the problem of pain is the strongest case against God, that much suffering is undeserved, and that a comfort can be invented because it's needed. What it offers isn't a proof but a claim you can weigh: that God didn't stay above suffering but entered it at the cross, and that the hope of a world made new rests on a tomb found empty. You don't have to accept that to notice it's stranger and more costly than the caricature, a God who wept and bled rather than one who watched.

faq.q: Someone I love is suffering right now. Can I use this to help me sit with them?
faq.a: Yes. The study is as much about being present to someone else's pain as bearing your own. Its most repeated lesson is the one that helps a companion most: resist the urge to explain or fix. Let the hard question be asked, weep with those who weep, and keep the path to real help visible when the pain is more than you can carry with them. You don't need answers to be present.

timeline.event: The book of Job takes up the problem of pain: a righteous man suffers for no reason he's ever told, protests to God's face, and is approved while the friends who explained are rebuked. The book's date is uncertain.
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple. Lamentations grieves the city in five poems that, at their center, call to mind the steadfast love of the LORD that never ceases.
Jesus is crucified, crying from the cross the first line of Psalm 22, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34).
Augustine develops his account of evil as privation, a lack or corruption of the good rather than a thing in itself, which shaped Western Christian thought on evil for centuries.
Gottfried Leibniz publishes his Theodicy, giving the word its modern use and arguing that ours is the best of all possible worlds.
An earthquake destroys Lisbon on All Saints' Day, November 1. Voltaire answers Leibniz's optimism with a poem on the disaster and later with Candide (1759).
C. S. Lewis publishes The Problem of Pain, a careful defense of belief in God in the face of suffering.

In prison letters of 1944, Dietrich Bonhoeffer writes that only a suffering God can help (paraphrased). He is executed in April 1945. His Ethics, published after his death, gives the church the language of the ultimate and the penultimate.
Elie Wiesel's memoir of Auschwitz and Buchenwald appears in French; the English translation, Night, follows in 1960.
C. S. Lewis publishes A Grief Observed, written after his wife's death, which at times reads like an argument with his earlier book.
Jürgen Moltmann publishes The Crucified God in German (English, 1974), drawing on the gallows scene in Night and arguing that God took human suffering into himself at the cross.
Nicholas Wolterstorff publishes Lament for a Son after his twenty-five-year-old son dies in a climbing accident.
Timothy Keller publishes Walking with God through Pain and Suffering.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here. It takes courage to talk about suffering in a room full of people. A few things before we start. First, this isn't a debate to win. It's something hard we're going to carry together, and the person in the most pain sets the pace. Second, we're not going to run on the cheap answers in here, like "everything happens for a reason," so if one slips out, we'll gently set it down and keep going. Third, when someone shares something real, our job is to hear it, not fix it. What's said here stays here. And one more thing, plainly. If anyone is carrying something that has grown too dark to hold alone, grief that won't lift, or a place where you've wondered whether you want to still be here, please tell me, tonight or privately. You don't have to carry that by yourself, and I'll help you find real help. You can also call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, at any hour. The God we're going to talk about wept at a grave. He doesn't ask anyone to suffer alone. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. Let me read our passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone speaks.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked closely at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, into the grief or fear each of us walked in carrying, because none of this matters if it stays a discussion about suffering in general.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though nothing's resolved, because suffering isn't solved in an evening and this study won't tie a bow on it. Try the practice this week, even haltingly. Remember what I said at the start: my door is open if you're carrying something too heavy, and there's no shame at all in reaching for help. Let me pray for us, and then I'll see you next time.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set ground rules about not fixing each other and not using the cheap answers, name where help can be found for anyone in crisis, and walk slowly through session 1's opening question.
Week 2: Session 1, The Question We Are Not Allowed to Ask, with extra time on Job.
Week 3: Session 2, Permission to Complain to God, praying a lament psalm together.
Week 4: Session 3, A God Who Does Not Explain, but Comes, part one: the cross as God's entry into godforsakenness.
Week 5: Session 3, part two: whether a suffering God is a weak God, and what it means that God has been in the dark before us.
Week 6: Session 4, The Thorn That Was Not Removed, refusing the formula and honoring those whose thorn remains.
Week 7: Session 5, Every Tear, and Whose Hand Wipes It.
Week 8: Looking back. Revisit the practices and memory verses, talk about what each person is carrying home, and make sure anyone who needs more help knows where to find it.

bibliography.title: Walking with God through Pain and Suffering
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: Published in 2013. Looks at how different cultures have tried to make sense of pain and sets out the Christian account. Background for sessions 1 and 4.

bibliography.title: The Crucified God
bibliography.author: Jürgen Moltmann
bibliography.note: Published in German in 1972 and in English in 1974. Argues that God took human suffering into himself at the cross, drawing on the gallows scene in Wiesel's Night. Moltmann began to come to faith as a prisoner of war. A demanding book; its claims about God's suffering are debated among faithful theologians. Background for session 3.

bibliography.title: The Problem of Pain
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Lewis's 1940 defense of belief in God in the face of suffering. Useful for stating the questions of session 1 clearly. Best read alongside A Grief Observed.

bibliography.title: A Grief Observed
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: The notebook Lewis kept after his wife's death, published in 1961. At times it reads like an argument with his earlier book. Supports sessions 1 and 2.

bibliography.title: Lament for a Son
bibliography.author: Nicholas Wolterstorff
bibliography.note: A father's reflections after his adult son's death in a climbing accident, published in 1987. Not a textbook; a companion for the grieving. Supports sessions 2 and 5.

bibliography.title: The Doors of the Sea: Where Was God in the Tsunami?
bibliography.author: David Bentley Hart
bibliography.note: A short, demanding book written after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, refusing both tidy theodicy and despair. Background for session 1.

bibliography.title: The Cross of Christ
bibliography.author: John Stott
bibliography.note: Published in 1986. A full treatment of the cross, including a well-known passage in which Stott says he could not believe in God were it not for the cross, and asks how one could worship a God immune to pain. Supports session 3.

bibliography.title: Night
bibliography.author: Elie Wiesel
bibliography.note: Wiesel's memoir of Auschwitz and Buchenwald. Moltmann draws on its gallows scene in The Crucified God. A witness from outside the Christian faith to the depth of the problem; handle it with reverence for the suffering it records.

bibliography.title: Letters and Papers from Prison
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Bonhoeffer's letters from Tegel prison, 1943 to 1945, including the 1944 letters in which he writes that only a suffering God can help. Background for session 3.

bibliography.title: Ethics
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Unfinished at his death and published afterward. Contains his distinction between the ultimate and the penultimate, which session 5 uses.

bibliography.title: Surprised by Hope
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: Published in 2008. Argues that biblical hope is resurrection and new creation, not escape to a disembodied heaven. Background for session 5.

bibliography.title: Job
bibliography.author: the book of Job
bibliography.note: The primary text of session 1. Read it straight through; it ends not with an explanation but with an encounter.

bibliography.title: The Book of Psalms
bibliography.author: the psalmists of Israel
bibliography.note: About a third are laments. Psalms 13, 22, 42, and 88 ground session 2, to be prayed and not only studied.

furtherReading: Walking with God through Pain and Suffering, Timothy Keller, for the fuller pastoral case behind sessions 1 and 4.
A Grief Observed, C. S. Lewis, for anyone in fresh grief who needs to see grief and faith on the same page.
Lament for a Son, Nicholas Wolterstorff, for those willing to sit with a father's grief.
The Crucified God, Jürgen Moltmann, for readers ready for a demanding theological case that God entered suffering himself.
Job, read straight through, to watch the Bible refuse the tidy answer and end in an encounter with God.

glossary.definition: An attempt to justify God in the face of evil and suffering. The word comes from Leibniz's book of 1710. The study takes the problem seriously but, like Job, doesn't offer a tidy theodicy as the answer.
The oldest and heaviest objection to belief in God: a world with this much undeserved suffering is hard to square with a God who is both perfectly good and fully able to stop it.
Prayer that brings grief, protest, and accusation directly to God while holding on to him, as in about a third of the Psalms. Different from grumbling, which talks about God to others and lets go.
The thread of Scripture, through Job, the lament psalms, Jeremiah, and Habakkuk, that puts the hard question to God directly and is approved rather than rebuked for it.
The experience of abandonment by God. At the cross Christ entered it, crying "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34), so no forsaken person is anywhere God hasn't been.

The classical teaching that God in his divine nature is not subject to suffering or change, held to guard his perfection and freedom. The study sets it beside the cross and holds the tension rather than collapsing it.
The title of Jürgen Moltmann's 1972 book, and shorthand for the claim that God didn't stay above human suffering but took it into himself at the cross.

Paul's name for an unnamed affliction he begged God three times to remove (2 Corinthians 12:7-8). It stayed. Because Scripture never says what it was, anyone with a wound that won't heal can find themselves in it.
God's answer to Paul: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Not removal or explanation, but grace given in the affliction.
The biblical hope: not escape to a disembodied heaven but heaven coming down, a renewed heaven and earth where God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:1-4).
Bonhoeffer's word, from his Ethics, for the next-to-last things that fill the time before God's final word. Present suffering is penultimate: real and painful, but not final.
Two things a sufferer might be offered. God mostly gives the first rather than the second: presence rather than a reason, company in the dark rather than an account of why it's dark.
Hebrew for God's steadfast, covenant love, which Lamentations says "never ceases" (Lamentations 3:22). The sufferer calls it to mind alongside the affliction, not instead of it.

God's governing of all things, including what he permits to wound us. The study refuses both the formula that reads every pain as a coded blessing and the despair that reads God's permission of suffering as his absence.
